title: TB8-19148
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I dismiss this appeal. XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant), XXXX XXXX XXXX (Second Appellant), XXXX XXXX XXXX (Third Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXX (Minor Appellant) are citizens of Nigeria. a. The Appellants fear persecution based upon the Third Appellant's sexual orientation as a bisexual man, which is known to their family, community, and the Nigerian police. The Third Appellant (TA) alleges two relationships with same-sex classmates in high school. The Appellants travelled to Canada in XXXX 2016 to attend the wedding of M, who is the daughter of the Principal Appellant (PA) and the Second Appellant (SA) and the TA's sister. After the wedding, the TA told M that he is bisexual. After M relayed this information to the PA and SA, the SA called their pastor in Nigeria to seek his support. The information about the TA's sexual orientation was spread amongst the church and was reported to the police. In XXXX 2017, police went to the Appellants' home looking for the TA as well as the rest of the Appellants, who are considered to be supportive of the TA. b. The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that the SA provided evasive and inconsistent testimony, that the PA omitted material information from the narrative, and that the TA's testimony was vague and lacking in basic detail. The Appellants argue the RPD erred in some of the credibility findings and that they relied upon their previous legal counsel in completing their narrative and application forms. c. The determinative issue is credibility. d. The RPD did not err in assessing the credibility of the PA, SA, and TA. The SA's testimony was inconsistent and evolving and the material omissions from the narrative are not reasonably explained. There is insufficient evidence to establish the TA's sexual orientation.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

In their memorandum, the Appellants indicate that they have submitted the following as new evidence: a letter from the XXXX XXXX Women's Centre and a police report from the Nigerian Divisional Police. In addition, the Appellants' record contains an affidavit from the Appellants' neighbor, IJ, sworn XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018.

According to the law,1 I can only accept evidence that: i. arose after the RPD decision; or ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or iii. that one could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.2 Letter from XXXX XXXX Women's Centre

On review of the Appellants' record, no letter from the XXXX XXXX Women's Centre was found. The Appellants were notified3 and given a short period of time in which to provide the letter referred to in their memorandum. No response was received. Affidavit of IJ is not admitted

The document is an affidavit of IJ sworn on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018. In the affidavit, IJ states that his second name was wrongly entered in his XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017 letter to the Appellants as "XXXX". He further states that the proper spelling of his second name is "XXXX" as found in his passport.

The affidavit is not referred to in the Appellants' memorandum as new evidence they have submitted, nor are there any submissions on how the affidavit was received or how it meets the criteria for admission.

The affidavit is sworn after the RPD decision on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018. The content of the affidavit does not make reference to when IJ became aware that his XXXX 2017 letter misspelled his middle name, and therefore it is impossible to assess whether this event occurred prior to or after the RPD decision.

I note that the Appellants' make the following statement in reference to the RPD's finding that IJ's letter was not reliable: The claimants explained that there was just one spelling letter error and that it could have been a spelling error while typing out the letter. The claimants did call XXXX after the hearing and was told that he did not proof read the letter before sending it off for the hearing.4 [emphasis added]

While this statement is contained in submissions, it clearly offers new information that is not in the form of a written statement or affidavit from the Appellants and there are no submissions provided as to its admissibility. The statement does, however, suggest that the Appellants contacted IJ after the hearing about the spelling of his name. I note that the hearing was held on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 and the decision was released on July 20, 2018. This demonstrates that the information in IJ's affidavit could possibly have been provided to the RPD prior to the release of the decision.

Nonetheless, given the lack of reference to the new affidavit and the fact that no submissions were provided about how the evidence meets the criteria under subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), I am unable to assess whether the affidavit is admissible. As the Federal Court has made clear: The burden of establishing the admissibility of new evidence lies on the appellant, necessitating full and detailed submissions on its admissibility and relevance. ...the RAD cannot be faulted for failing to decide an issue that was not properly argued.5
The affidavit is not admitted. Invitation letter/warrant for arrest is not admitted

Although described by the Appellants as a police report, the document consists of a one-page invitation letter6 and an attached one-page warrant for arrest.7 The invitation letter is from the Nigerian Police Force, Divisional Police in XXXX, Delta State, dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018. The letter is addressed to the TA at his last Nigerian home address in XXXX and requests that he attend to the police station by XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, in relation to a report that he committed an unnatural offence under the criminal code. The warrant for arrest indicates that the TA has been charged with committing an unnatural offence under the criminal code and is dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018. The warrant commands that the TA be brought before the Magistrate's Court in XXXX.

In their memorandum, the Appellants state that the "police report" indicates that the TA is still wanted for arrest by the police. I note that the Appellants have not provided a written statement or sworn affidavit that provides information about how, when and from whom the Appellants received the documents.

The invitation letter and warrant are both dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, and therefore clearly arose after the RPD decision on July 20, 2018. As such, the documents meet the requirements of subsection 110(4). The documents are new and are also relevant to the ongoing threat of persecution alleged by the Appellants.

As to whether the invitation letter and warrant are credible, I note that the documents are not originals, rather, they are photocopies of somewhat poor quality. I also note several discrepancies in the documents.

First, the letterhead on the invitation letter appears to contain a typographical or spelling error in the title - "Divisional Police Headquarter" - when one would expect it to be titled "Headquarters" [emphasis added]. The official stamp also refers to the "Divisional Police Hqtrs". In comparison to examples provided in the country documentation,8 I note the Nigeria Police Force crest is of a smaller size and placed on the left of the document rather than in the centre of the letterhead. Finally, I also note that the same country documentation indicates this type of invitation letter is "'usually signed by a superior police officer from the rank of cadet Assistant Superintendent of Police (ASP).'"9 In comparison, the warrant submitted by the Appellants indicates it is signed by "ASP XXXX XXXX, Admin Officer for Divisional Police Officer, XXXX."10

In terms of the warrant, I note that it has been completed in handwriting on a typewritten criminal procedure form. The title of the form is as follows: FORM NO. 6 (Section 97) Warrant for apprehension of defendant in first instance

In comparison, Form No. 6 in Schedule 1 of the current Nigerian Administration of Criminal Justice Act, 201511 (ACJA) contains the following title: FORM NO. 6 (Section 132) Warrant for arrest of defendant in first instance [emphasis added]

I also note that a handwritten portion of the form directs "all members of the court" to bring the TA before the Magistrate's Court in XXXX. Section 36 of the ACJA provides the following requirements for a warrant of arrest: (1) A warrant of arrest issued under this Act, unless the contrary is expressly provided under any other law, shall: (a) bear the date of the day of issue; (b) contain all necessary particulars; and (c) be signed by the Judge or Magistrate by whom it is issued. (2) A warrant shall state concisely the offence or matter for which it is issued and shall name or otherwise describe the suspect to be arrested, and it shall order the police officer or officers to whom it is directed to arrest the suspect and bring him before the court to answer the complaint or statement, or to testify or be dealt with according to the circumstances of the case, and to be further dealt with according to law. [emphasis added]

This section confirms general knowledge that a warrant is signed by a judge to provide authority and direction to the police to arrest an individual - a warrant is not directed at members of the court. A further observation is that the form is incomplete as it does not contain the date of the oath on which the charge was based. The date entered to reference the year of the alleged offence is overwritten and it is impossible to discern whether it is 2017, 2018 or 2019. Finally, although there is a signature by a Magistrate, the Magistrate Court stamp is unsigned and undated.

Given the multiple discrepancies I have noted and the lack of information as to how the documents were received by the Appellants, I find the invitation letter and warrant are not credible on their face and are more likely than not fraudulent documents. The invitation letter and warrant are not admitted. Request for oral hearing is denied
As no new evidence has been admitted, I have no jurisdiction to hold an oral hearing. The request for an oral hearing is denied.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.12 SA's testimony about arrest warrant is unresponsive

The RPD found that the SA's testimony about the existence of an arrest warrant was evasive. The Appellants argue that the SA explained in her testimony that her neighbor, IJ, was questioned by the police and that the pastor had called IJ and "saw a document from the police indicating their warrant."13 I disagree.

In the Appellants' narrative, they state that they learned that the police had come to their home to arrest them on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017. At the hearing, the TA testified that he did not know whether a formal arrest warrant had been issued. The SA testified that she knew an arrest warrant had been issued from IJ. In follow-up, the SA testified as follows: MEMBER: Okay, now I asked this to your son before, but as far as you know, is there a warrant for your arrest? CLAIMANT 2: Yes. MEMBER: Okay, and how do you know that? CLAIMANT 2: They went to, someone in my church went to the police station to make a report. MEMBER: Okay, and that doesn't necessarily mean that there is a warrant for your arrest. So how do you know that there has been a warrant that has been issued by the police for your arrest? CLAIMANT 2: They went to my house to carry out an arrest for me and my family. MEMBER: Do you know what a warrant is for your arrest? Do you know what that is? CLAIMANT 2: Yes, they want to arrest us because of the bisexual thing that my son is involved. MEMBER: Okay, has anyone informed you whether or not there is a document, a warrant? CLAIMANT 2: Yes, our neighbour. MEMBER: What about your neighbour? CLAIMANT 2: The day the police went for an arrest in my house, they went everywhere, they got in [they bust] into the house. MEMBER: Okay, but did anyone ever tell you there is a warrant for your arrest, convey that information to you so that there is. Just wait for me to finish, okay. Or are you assuming that there is a warrant for your arrest because there has been a search of your home? CLAIMANT 2: Yes, someone told us that the police are after us for an arrest. MEMBER: Okay, but nobody has told you specifically using the sentence there is a warrant for your arrest. Is that correct? CLAIMANT 2: Israel Jacob. The police they went to him because he stayed next to our flat. So they went to him and asked him about us, and they told him that "these people, their son is practicing a wrong thing and we need them, where are they?"14

I have carefully reviewed the hearing transcript as well as the audio recording and do not agree with the Appellants' that the SA testified that the pastor saw a document from the police when he visited IJ. In my view, the SA was given multiple opportunities to directly answer whether she understood what an arrest warrant was, whether she was assuming one had been issued because the police came to their home, and why she was sure an arrest warrant had been issued. Yet the SA maintained that IJ told her that there was a warrant for their arrest and provided no further detail or explanation. Given the centrality of this issue to the Appellants' allegations, I find the SA's resistance to answer the RPD's direct questions concerning. The SA's failure to provide reasonable detail about a material element of the Appellants' claim also causes concern as to the reliability of her testimony. The RPD did not err in finding the SA was evasive and unresponsive in her testimony. I draw a negative inference as to the SA's credibility. Neighbor's letter does not reference arrest warrant

The RPD found that the SA provided inconsistent testimony about how IJ came to write a letter to them and noted a discrepancy in the spelling of IJ's name on the letter. The RPD noted the letter did not refer to an arrest warrant and concluded the letter was unreliable. The Appellants argue that the error could have been a typographical error but make no further arguments about the RPD's conclusion.

The letter from IJ to the Appellants is brief and casual in tone, indicating that the situation is very tense and that the police and youths are coming by to check if they have come back to Nigeria. A copy of his passport is attached. There is no mention of an arrest warrant or other police document. When initially asked by the RPD, the SA said that IJ did not know that the Appellants were seeking asylum in Canada. Later, in response to the RPD's question as to why IJ would attach a copy of his passport to the letter if he didn't know about their refugee claim, the SA said that her pastor told IJ they were making a claim. IJ offered to give the pastor a copy of the letter to be included with other documents sent to the Appellants. When the RPD pointed out to the SA that this was inconsistent with her testimony that IJ did not know about their asylum claim, she did not provide an explanation. The RPD did not err in finding the SA's testimony was inconsistent and not reasonably explained.

The Appellants argue that it is possible that the misspelling of IJ's second name is merely a typographical error; I agree. On its own, it would be insufficient to consider IJ's letter as unreliable. However, in combination with the inconsistencies in SA's testimony as to how the letter came into existence, there is sufficient concern to question its reliability. Most notably, the letter makes no reference to any police document. As such, I concur with the RPD's finding that, on a balance of probabilities, no arrest warrant has been issued for the Appellants. Omissions from narrative are material and not reasonably explained

The RPD found that the Appellants made material omissions in their narrative. The Appellants' argue that they relied on their previous legal counsel to assist them in completing their narrative and application forms and the RPD's conclusions are in error. I disagree.

When allegations are made against former counsel, the Immigration Refugee Board (IRB) Practice notice provides procedural steps that must be taken: 6. Where the person alleges that they have been inadequately represented by their former counsel, the person must first provide former counsel with: a. a written statement containing the allegations, or in the case of an appeal to the RAD, a copy of the Appellant's Memorandum or other document in the RAD proceedings that contain the allegations; and b. a written notice that former counsel has ten days after receiving the allegations to provide a written response to the person, to the applicable Division, and to the Minister (if the Minister is a party to the proceeding); and c. a signed authorization releasing any privilege, including solicitor-client privilege, to the extent necessary to allow former counsel to respond to the allegations; and d. a copy of this Practice Notice or information describing where this Practice Notice can be found on the IRB website. 7. The person must then provide to the Division a copy of documents (a) to (c) above, as well as proof that the documents (a) to (d) above have been provided to the person's former counsel. 8. Former counsel who intends to respond to the allegations must provide a written response to the person, to the Division, and to the Minister (if the Minister is a party to the proceeding), no later than ten days after receiving the allegations. 9. The person may provide a written reply to the Division, accompanied by proof that this reply was first provided to former counsel and to the Minister (if the Minister is a party to the proceeding). The written reply must be provided no later than five days after the person received former counsel's response.15

In my review of the Appellants' record, I do not find any reference to the above-noted practice note nor any documents that would demonstrate that the required procedural steps have been taken. As such, I am not satisfied that former counsel has been given the opportunity to respond to the allegations. Absent this requirement, the Appellants' allegations of inadequate representation must fail.

Following my independent review, I find that the RPD was correct in identifying material omissions in the Appellants' narrative and their application forms. I note that in response to a question about whether they have ever been arrested or sought by police, the Appellants answered no. I also note that the Appellants' narrative does not mention the two adult children of the PA and SA, whom the SA testified are in hiding because the police are searching for the entire family. These omissions are central to the Appellants' allegations and no reasonable explanation was provided. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the police do not have information that the TA is bisexual, and that the police are not looking for the Appellants. Insufficient evidence to establish TA's sexual orientation

The RPD found that the TA's testimony about his previous same-sex relationships was vague and lacking in basic detail. The Appellant argues that the TA "indicated that he felt uncomfortable describing his relationships [in] front of his family at the hearing."16 I disagree.

Having carefully reviewed the record as well as the audio recording, I note that the RPD directly asked the TA if there was anything that he didn't want to be asked about with his family present: MEMBER: Okay, now I am concerned of the fact that I am asking you these personal questions in front of your family. Mister, anything that you don't want to be asked in front of your family, I realise we are kind of in front of family right now. CLAIMANT 3: I think its okay. It's okay.17
The TA was represented by legal counsel throughout the entirety of the hearing. No further reference to this issue is made in the remainder of the hearing, including the submissions of legal counsel.

Given that the issue was directly raised by the RPD, the TA's response was that it was okay and he in fact continued to testify, it is difficult to accept the Appellants' argument. He was duly represented by legal counsel throughout the hearing and prior to the release of the RPD decision and no concern was raised about this issue. I find the Appellants' argument to be without basis.

I note that the Appellants have not raised any further argument about the RPD's conclusion that there is insufficient evidence to establish the TA's sexual orientation. I have independently reviewed the record in relation to these findings and find no error in the RPD's findings. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the TA's sexual orientation is not bisexual.
Based on the above conclusions, there is insufficient credible information to establish that the Appellants face a serious possibility of persecution or a risk of harm if they return to Nigeria.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
